opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. To me, intelligence in embodied intelligence has two layers that are deeply connected but quite different in character.

The first layer is what I'd call high-level reasoning, or semantic intelligence. That's understanding the world, understanding what a person is asking you to do, breaking a long task into steps, and knowing, for example, that if you're asked to clean up a table, the cup goes in the sink and the trash goes in the bin. Over the past few years, large language models and vision-language models have made enormous progress here. A lot of this common-sense knowledge can now be transferred from internet-scale data into robots, which was unimaginable not long ago.

The second layer is physical intelligence: dexterity, motor control, the ability to actually interact with the physical world. Grasping a soft object, tying a shoelace, inserting a plug, keeping balance when someone pushes you. Interestingly, this is the part we humans take for granted, but it's actually the harder one for robots. It's the classic Moravec's paradox: things that are easy for a three-year-old, like picking up a toy, are extremely hard for machines, while things that are hard for us, like chess or math, turned out to be relatively easier for computers.

Why is physical intelligence so hard? One reason is data. For language and images we have the whole internet, but there's no internet of robot actions. The physical world is also continuous, high-dimensional, and full of contact and friction that are hard to model. And the feedback loop is very tight. You can't think for ten seconds before deciding how to adjust your fingers when a cup starts slipping.

So my view is that true embodied intelligence requires both. Reasoning without dexterity gives you a robot that knows exactly what to do but can't do it. Dexterity without reasoning gives you a very skillful machine that doesn't understand why it's doing anything. The exciting direction now is bringing these two together in one model, so the robot can understand, plan, and act in a unified way, and so that knowledge from the digital world can really ground itself in the physical world. I think closing the gap on the physical side is the main bottleneck right now, and it's where a lot of the most interesting research is happening.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes both high-level reasoning and physical intelligence, explicitly including dexterity and motor control, and says embodied intelligence requires both.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and it's actually one I think about a lot, because the word "intelligence" in embodied intelligence gets used very loosely.

The way I see it, there are really two layers. One is what people usually mean by intelligence: reasoning, planning, understanding language, understanding the world semantically. If I tell a robot, "clean up the kitchen," it needs to know what counts as clean, what a dish is, that the dish goes in the sink and not in the trash, and in what order to do things. That is high-level cognition, and the big foundation models have made enormous progress there. A lot of that knowledge can transfer from the internet, from text and video, into robots.

The other layer is physical dexterity: actually grasping the slippery plate, not dropping it, adjusting when it slides in your hand, walking over an uneven floor while carrying it. And I'd argue that this is also intelligence, even though people tend not to call it that. It's just intelligence that evolution spent hundreds of millions of years on, and so it feels effortless to us. This is the old Moravec's paradox. A five-year-old can do things with their hands that no robot can do today, while a robot can already hold a better conversation about physics than most adults.

What I find interesting is that these two layers have very different data stories. For reasoning, we have essentially the whole internet. For dexterity, there is no internet of touch, no internet of contact forces and muscle commands. So we have to generate that data ourselves, through simulation, through teleoperation, through robots practicing in the real world. That's why in my own work I lean so heavily on simulation and reinforcement learning for the low-level skills, especially for locomotion. Simulation lets you have thousands of robots falling down and getting back up in parallel, which no lab could afford physically.

But I don't think you can treat them as two separate problems that you solve independently and then glue together. Dexterity feeds reasoning. When a child manipulates objects, they are learning physics, they are learning concepts like "heavy," "fragile," "stuck." A lot of common sense is grounded in the body. Conversely, reasoning makes dexterity useful: a very agile robot that doesn't know what to do is just an expensive toy.

So my honest answer is that intelligence in embodied intelligence is the ability to close the loop between the two. Perceive the physical world, decide what to do at a semantic level, and then execute it with the kind of fast, adaptive, robust control that our bodies do without thinking. Right now the top layer is advancing faster than the bottom layer, and I think the bottom layer, physical competence, is the real bottleneck for getting robots into homes. Which is also why I find it the most exciting part to work on.

r001.rationale: The response identifies both high-level reasoning and physical dexterity as layers of intelligence, and explicitly says physical dexterity is also intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think intelligence has at least two aspects. One is the ability to reason—to understand a situation, make a plan, and decide what to do. The other is the ability to interact with the physical world. That includes perception, coordination, and dexterity.

We tend to recognize the first kind more easily. When we see someone solve a difficult math problem, we say, “That’s intelligent.” But picking up a cup, walking across uneven ground, or catching a ball also requires intelligence. Those actions seem simple because we do them almost without thinking. For a robot, they involve handling uncertainty and continuously adapting to what happens.

Embodied intelligence brings these two aspects together. If you want a robot to make a cup of coffee, it needs to figure out the steps, but it also needs to grasp the cup, control the pouring, and respond if something slips. A good plan is useful only if the robot can carry it out, and what it senses during execution may require it to change the plan. To me, that connection between reasoning and physical action is central.

r001.rationale: The response identifies reasoning as one aspect of intelligence and physical-world interaction, including coordination and dexterity, as the other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think intelligence has at least two closely related aspects. One is reasoning: understanding a task, making a plan, and deciding what to do. The other is physical dexterity: actually interacting with the world and making that plan work.

For a robot, the connection between them is crucial. You might tell it, “Clean up this table.” It needs to understand what belongs where, but it also needs to grasp objects, handle different weights and shapes, and adjust when something slips. A good plan alone doesn’t solve the task, and dexterous movement alone doesn’t tell you what task to perform.

So I see embodied intelligence as bringing these capabilities together through interaction. The robot acts, observes what happens, and updates its decisions. Reasoning guides action, and physical experience informs reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response identifies reasoning as understanding tasks and planning, and physical dexterity as interacting with the world and carrying out plans.
